arguments.text: Lisbon is struggling with the strain of being a top European tourist destination. Rents in historic neighborhoods like Alfama and Graça have doubled since 2016, displacing long-time residents and replacing local amenities with tourist-focused businesses. While the city council has attempted to intervene with measures like license freezes on short-term rentals, these are often delayed by legal challenges from owners' groups. Many residents have been forced to move to the periphery, resulting in longer commutes that will not be improved by transit projects until at least 2030. These housing issues are interconnected with broader infrastructure challenges, including water shortages, airport capacity, and transport limits, forcing a difficult debate over how many visitors the city can sustainably support. The mayor advocates for a shift toward fewer, higher-spending tourists, though industry groups remain concerned about the economic consequences.
